title: The Treasure by the Stream
summary: On a rainy day, three children find a map in the attic that their grandpa drew when he was a boy. The next day, they set off into the woods to look for the X by the stream.

scenes.text:
It had been raining since the morning.

Nina, Mateo and Bea had already played everything. Hide-and-seek, pirates, guessing shapes in the grey clouds. There was nothing left to invent.

"We're sooo bored," said Nina, with her forehead pressed against the window.

Mum, who was folding the washing, nodded towards the ceiling.

"There are boxes in the attic that nobody's opened for years."

All three of them lit up.

They climbed the narrow stairs, one behind the other. At the top there was a small door with a rusty latch.

Nina pushed it with her shoulder. And it opened with a groan.

The attic was like a whole country hidden under the roof.

There was a three-legged chair, a trunk with golden buckles, a lamp with no bulb and mountains of boxes. It smelled of old paper and stored-away wool.

Bea found a straw hat and put it on crooked. Mateo found a toy soldier with one arm missing. Nina opened a box full of black-and-white photos.

And at the bottom of the trunk, under a blue scarf, there was a little wooden box, tied up with string.

Inside was a piece of paper folded into four, yellow at the edges, as soft as a dry leaf.

They spread it out on the floor, very carefully.

It was a map, drawn by hand in pencil and crayon. It had pine trees, a log bridge and a wiggly blue line. And at the end, next to an enormous tree, a red X.

At the bottom, in big, wobbly writing, it said:

"For whoever has a brave heart. Ramón, aged 9."

"It's Grandpa!" whispered Mateo. "Grandpa hid a treasure when he was a boy!"

"This is behind the woods," said Nina, following the blue line with her finger. "Dad took us there once."

Bea looked at the X very seriously, with enormous eyes.

"What if we go and look for it? Tomorrow."

That night, the three of them huddled under a sheet with a torch, like real explorers.

They packed their backpacks: bread, three apples, a water bottle, a ball of string, a spoon for digging and Grandpa's map, folded up safely in the front pocket.

Bea packed her rag rabbit too. An explorer doesn't abandon anyone.

"We leave at dawn," said Nina.

Outside, the rain slowly stopped. And Bea fell asleep with her boots on.

The sky was only just turning pink when they set off.

They left a note on the table: "Gone on an important mission. Back for lunch."

Everything sparkled with dew, as if the rain had left the world freshly washed. They crossed the meadow in their wet boots and went into the woods.

Up above, the birds were waking one by one, until the whole wood was singing.

"Is it much further?" asked Bea.

"Just far enough," said Nina, studying the map the way a captain studies the sea.

And then, through the trees, they heard it. A happy murmur that never stopped.

The stream!

The water ran clear between round stones. It was so cold that when they dipped their hands in, it set them off giggling.

"The first clue is 'where the water sits down to rest'," read Nina.

They searched for a good while. Until Mateo found a still pool, round as a plate, where the water calmed down and the whole sky was reflected in it.

And there, half covered in moss, was a flat stone with a yellow sun painted on it.

The paint was ancient, worn away by lots of rain. But you could still see it.

"Grandpa painted that!" shouted Mateo.

Next to the stone, someone had laid out pebbles in a row, making an arrow that pointed upwards, following the water.

Further on there was no bridge. Just some big, slippery stones poking out of the water, like turtles' backs.

"Step where I step," said Nina.

She went across slowly, arms out like a tightrope walker. Mateo followed her, counting the stones out loud.

Bea reached the middle one and froze.

"It's too far," she said quietly.

"I'm right here," said Mateo, and held out his hand.

Bea jumped. She nearly made it. But her left boot landed in the water. Splosh!

It splashed her right up to her ears.

There was a second of silence. And then the three of them burst out laughing on the bank, with one boot dripping and the sun warming their backs.

But past the water, the path split in two. And the map was no help at all: Grandpa's line ended in a smudge, as if the pencil had got tired.

"It's left," said Nina.

"It's right," said Mateo. "Can't you see the crooked pine from the drawing?"

"That pine isn't crooked. It's leaning."

"Same thing!"

They walked one way. They came back. They walked the other way. They kept talking louder and louder, and their words came out with sharp points.

Bea sat down on a root, hugging her rabbit, and didn't say anything.

And nobody asked her anything, because the two big ones were far too busy being right.

While the big ones argued, Bea looked at the ground. It was her favourite thing to look at.

And she saw something strange. Poking up through the forest floor was the tip of a grey stone, far too neat to be there by accident.

Slowly, like someone opening a present, she brushed away the leaves.

Underneath were three stones piled one on top of another. And on the top one, scratched with a nail, was a tiny sun.

"Nina," said Bea. "Mateo."

Nobody heard her.

So she filled her chest with air and shouted with all her might:

"THERE'S A SUN HERE!"

The two big ones spun round at the same time. They hurried over and crouched down to look.

It was true. It was Grandpa's sign. It had been waiting for them for years and years, right beside the path that neither of them had wanted to look at.

"Sorry, Bea," said Nina, going red. "We weren't listening to you."

"Sorry," said Mateo.

Bea shrugged, happy, and showed them the sun again, just in case.

From then on they were a real team. Nina read the map. Mateo held back the branches so the others could get through. And Bea, the one who looked at the ground, found the signs.

She found two more. And on the last slope, with their backpacks bouncing, the three of them broke into a run.

And there it was: the tree from the drawing.

It was an enormous oak, with a trunk as wide as a table. In the bark there was an old X, which the tree had slowly hugged into itself over the years.

They dug with whatever they had: the spoon, two sticks and their hands. The earth was damp and smelled of roots.

Until Mateo's stick hit something hard. Clunk!

They dug faster. A corner appeared. Then an edge. Then a whole lid.

It was a small wooden chest, the size of a shoebox, with a rusty iron clasp.

The three of them looked at each other. And they opened it together.

There were no gold coins. There were no necklaces.

There were things that gleamed even brighter.

A blue marble that seemed to have a sea inside it. A wooden whistle. A handful of bottle tops, shining like coins. A photo of a skinny boy with a fishing rod, and on the back, written in pencil: "Ramón and the fish that got away."

And a folded piece of paper that said:

"If you've found this, you're already a bit of an adventurer. Look after it."

Nina read it twice, and her eyes filled with tears, the good kind.

"Grandpa was just like us," said Bea, holding the marble up to the sun.

They got home just as the sun was going down.

Mum was waiting at the door, with a face that said "we'll talk about this later." But on the porch, in his usual chair, with a blanket over his knees, sat Grandpa Ramón.

Bea put the chest in his lap.

Grandpa looked at it for a long while, without saying a word.

"It can't be," he said at last, very quietly. "I buried this when I was nine."

He took out the blue marble, and his eyes crinkled up from smiling so much. And he told them, one by one, about all his treasures. The fish that got away. The whistle he made with his dad. The bottle tops he collected one whole summer.

The three of them listened without moving, until night fell.

That night, after their bath and their soup, the three of them went to bed with cheeks still warm from the sun.

The chest stayed open on the bedside table, with the blue marble on top of everything.

"I thought the treasure would be coins," said Bea, her voice full of sleep.

"This is better," said Mateo. "It's Grandpa when he was a boy."

Nina thought for a while. And she said the last true thing of the day:

"The treasure was the whole day. And the three of us."

But nobody heard it. Bea and Mateo were already asleep.
